say: Welcome back, inquirers! A triangle is half of something. Today we find out half of WHAT, and why a squashed, leaning triangle can have exactly the same area as a neat one.
Notice it, test it, explain why. Today “test it” means cutting paper.
Here are three rectangles, each with a shaded triangle. Thumbs up if you think the triangle is exactly half of the rectangle, thumbs down if not. Decide for each one before I click.
For the one that is not half: how much of the rectangle is it? How do you know?
You will draw a rectangle 8 cm by 6 cm and a triangle inside it with its top corner on the top side. Predict: what fraction of the rectangle is the triangle? Does it matter where the top corner is?
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: fold each leftover piece along a grid line and lay it on the triangle.
Pieces do not fit: check that your top corner is exactly on the top side and the bottom corners are the rectangle’s corners.
If a pair wants more: move the top corner right to the end of the top side. What kind of triangle is it now? Is it still half?

say: “This triangle has sides 5, 12 and 13. Which two do I multiply? The height must meet the base at a right angle. I look for the square corner: 12 and 5 meet there. 13 is slanting, so I do not use it. 1/2 × 12 × 5 = 30.”

“Here the top corner is past the end of the base. I extend the base with a dashed line and drop the height to it: 12 cm. The base is still only 11 cm: the dashed part is not part of the triangle. 1/2 × 11 × 12 = 66.”

“All three triangles sit on the bottom of the same rectangle with their top corner on the top side. Same base, 14 cm. Same height, 9 cm. So they all have the same area, 63 cm², even though they look different.”

do: Ask: “Point to the height. How do you know it meets the base at a right angle?”
Ask: “Which length did you not need? Why not?”
Ask: “Did you split the figure or take away? Could you do it the other way to check?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Find the square corner (the right angle). The two lines that make it are a base and a height.”
Hint 2: “If there is no square corner, look for a dashed line drawn at a right angle to a side.”
Hint 3: “Box the shape in a rectangle. Find the rectangle’s area, then take away the white triangles.”

do: Ask: “Point to the height. How do you know it meets the base at a right angle?”
Ask: “Which length did you not need? Why not?”
Ask: “Did you split the figure or take away? Could you do it the other way to check?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Find the square corner (the right angle). The two lines that make it are a base and a height.”
Hint 2: “If there is no square corner, look for a dashed line drawn at a right angle to a side.”
Hint 3: “Box the shape in a rectangle. Find the rectangle’s area, then take away the white triangles.”

say: “Ben says a triangle with longer sides always has a bigger area. Is he right?”
“How can two triangles that look very different have the same area?”
ask: “Ben says a triangle with longer sides always has a bigger area. Is he right?”

No. Two triangles with the same base and the same height have the same area, even if one leans over and has much longer sides. The area depends on the base and the height, not on the slanting sides. A very long, thin triangle can even have a smaller area than a short, wide one.

say: “Today you found the height (sometimes outside the triangle), and you saw why triangles on the same base with the same height have the same area. That is explaining why.”
“Show me your exit ticket and collect your stamp.”

p5l4-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Find the area of a triangle as 1/2 × base × height, choosing a base and the height that meets it at a right angle (also when the height is outside the triangle); use “same base, same height” to explain equal areas; find areas of composite figures and shaded parts by splitting into triangles or by taking away. Thinking strategies today: FIND THE BASE AND ITS HEIGHT, SAME BASE AND SAME HEIGHT, and SPLIT OR TAKE AWAY. Materials: Square grid paper (cut-out page at the back of the workbook) with an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle already drawn on it the day before, scissors, ruler, set square or the corner of a card, mini whiteboard and marker, workbook, pencil. Online: The tutor shares the slides and clicks to draw heights and reveal each step. For the explore, children draw and cut their rectangle with the camera up as usual, and check by laying the pieces together at home that they fit (or use the interactive version on the slide). Children write on whiteboards for the quick questions and say the answer together on three. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5 (one check for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6.5 to 12.5 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 12.5 to 25.5 (pair work 6.5 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 25.5 to 36.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36.5 to 41, workbook page 1 41 to 53.5 (the questions without a star; after question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 53.5 to 57, short teaching before page 2 57 to 60, workbook page 2 60 to 70 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 70 to 73, talk time 73 to 78.5 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 78.5 to 82, reflection 82 to 84.5 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 84.5 to 85.5, and the buffer 85.5 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." SPINE: Today's tool is Act it out. Model or simulate the situation (objects, fold, cut, dice) and record the outcomes. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p5l4-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE check for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three (face to face, you may glance at papers held low as you walk round; online, nothing is held up to the camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: 24 squares. The two triangles match exactly (turn one round and it fits on the other), so each is 1/2 of the rectangle: 12 squares.; Q2: No, 30 cm². The base DC = 12 cm and the height from P down to DC is always 5 cm, so the area is 1/2 × 12 × 5 = 30 cm² wherever P is. A guess of "it changes" is fine: we test it in the explore. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4.5 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: children say the answers together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE check for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l4-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 9. Half or not? Children vote with thumbs for each rectangle before you click. Answers: Rectangle 1 is half (a diagonal cuts a rectangle into two equal triangles). Rectangle 2 is half too: the top corner is on the top side, so the triangle has the whole bottom side as its base and the whole height of the rectangle as its height. Many children say no because the picture looks "pointy"; do not explain yet, collect reasons. Rectangle 3 is NOT half: the corner of the triangle is in the middle of the right side, so the triangle is 1/4 of the rectangle (base 12 cm, height 4 cm; 1/2 × 12 × 4 = 24 cm² out of 96 cm²). Say: "Hold on to your reasons. We will explain why."

p5l4-warm2.note: Minutes 9 to 12.5. Whiteboards: read each question aloud, give thinking time, write on boards, say the answer together on three, then click. Answers: 1) 42 cm² (7 × 6). 2) 21 cm² (half of 42). 3) 18 (9 × 4 = 36, half is 18). 4) 7 cm (7 × 7 = 49). Ask after 3: "What are we really doing when we halve? A triangle is half of a rectangle: which rectangle?" Listen for "the base times the height".

p5l4-explore1.note: Minutes 12.5 to 25.5 (the whole explore; this slide 12.5 to 21.5). Ask parents the day before to draw the 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle on the grid paper (it is on the materials list), so pairs only mark the point and cut out the three pieces (online: camera up as usual; check by laying the cut pieces together). Pair work is at most 6.5 minutes. Predict first: what fraction of the rectangle is the triangle? Does it matter where the point is? Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): put the point at the end of the top side. What kind of triangle is it now? Is it still half? (Yes: a right-angled triangle, half of the rectangle.) PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6.5 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 21.5 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: For example base 6 and height 4, base 8 and height 3, base 12 and height 2, base 4 and height 6. Each time base × height = 24, which is double the area (12 × 2). Any triangle on the same base and height, leaning or not, is also fine.

p5l4-explore2.note: Minutes 21.5 to 25.5. Gather the pairs. Lay the pieces together: the two blue pieces fit exactly on the yellow triangle. Answers: 1) Yes. Each blue piece is half of a smaller rectangle (cut it along the dashed line from the point down), so together the blue pieces equal the triangle. 2) 24 cm²: the rectangle is 8 × 6 = 48 cm² and the triangle is half. (Not asked together, but say it if nobody does) Does it matter where the point is? No: the base is always 8 cm and the height is always 6 cm, wherever the point is. Do NOT name the formula yet if nobody finds it; the next slide does. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): For example base 6 and height 4, base 8 and height 3, base 12 and height 2, base 4 and height 6. Each time base × height = 24, which is double the area (12 × 2). Any triangle on the same base and height, leaning or not, is also fine.

p5l4-teach1.note: Minutes 25.5 to 28. Teach. Ask first: "Which length is the height?" Let children argue; then show the square corner. Click order: step 1, step 2, step 3 (the dashed copy makes the rectangle). Think-aloud: "The height must meet the base at a right angle. Here the square corner tells me: 12 is the base and 5 is the height. 13 leans over, so it is not a height. Half of base times height: half of 60 is 30." Link back to the explore: the triangle is half of the rectangle 12 by 5. Common error: using 13 as the height (1/2 × 12 × 13 = 78: wrong).

p5l4-try1.note: Minutes 28 to 29. Whiteboards. a) 1/2 × 10 × 7 = 35. b) 1/2 × 9 × 12 = 54; 15 and 20 are the slanting sides. (Two items only.)

p5l4-teach2.note: Minutes 29 to 31.5. Teach. Ask: "Where is the height now? There is no square corner inside the triangle." Click order: step 1, the dashed extension and the height appear, steps 2 and 3, the answer. Think-aloud: "A height does not have to be inside. I extend the base with a dashed line, then draw a line from the top corner straight down to it, at a right angle. That is the height: 12 cm. But the base is only the 11 cm side. The area is half of 11 times 12: 66 cm². The 13 cm and 20 cm sides are not needed." Show it with a paper triangle leaning over. Common mistake: using the base plus the dashed part (16 cm).

p5l4-teach3.note: Minutes 31.5 to 33.5. Teach. Ask first: "Do the three triangles have the same area? They look different." Collect opinions, then click. Think-aloud: "Look at the dashed height in each: it is 9 cm every time, because the top corner is on the top side, which is 9 cm above the bottom side. The base is the same 14 cm. So 63 cm² each, half of the rectangle." Connect to the warm-up: Rectangle 2 was half because it was this exact situation. Ask: "What if the top corner is at the very end of the top side?" (a right-angled triangle, still 63.) And: "What if it moves beyond the rectangle, along the same top line?" (the height is still 9 cm: still 63).

p5l4-try2.note: Minutes 33.5 to 35. Whiteboards. a) 1/2 × 6 × 10 = 30 and 1/2 × 12 × 5 = 30: the same area, although the shapes are very different. b) Half of 8 × 5 = 40, so 20 cm². (Two items only.)

p5l4-key.note: Minutes 35 to 36.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Using a slanting side as the height (1/2 × 14 × 13 for a 13-14-15 triangle). (2) Forgetting the 1/2 and giving the area of the whole rectangle. (3) For a height outside the triangle, measuring the base all the way to the foot of the height (adding the dashed extension to the base).

p5l4-break.note: Minutes 36.5 to 41. 4.5 minutes. Online: children stand in view of the camera. Make a triangle with both arms above the head. Make a right angle with one arm. Then lean the triangle left and right: the height does not change. Then a drink of water.

p5l4-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 53.5. Walk around. Ask "Which line is the height? How do you know?" before giving any help. Q1b: children often use 13 or 15 as the height; point to the dashed line. Q1c: the height is OUTSIDE the triangle and the base is only 9 cm (the dashed part is not in the triangle). Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 2 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 and Q2. Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l4-ws1ans.note: Minutes 53.5 to 57. Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1a: 1/2 × 8 × 6 = 24 (the 10 cm side is slanting). Q1b: 1/2 × 14 × 12 = 84. Q1c: 1/2 × 9 × 8 = 36 (the 17 cm side is not needed). Q2: P and Q are on AB, which is 6 cm above DC, so both triangles have base 10 cm and height 6 cm. Each is half of the 60 cm² rectangle.

p5l4-teachtake.note: Minutes 57 to 58.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Ask: "The shaded triangle has no square corner and no side along the rectangle. Can we find its base and height directly?" (Hard.) "What do we know? The three white triangles each have a square corner." Click through. Think-aloud: "I find the whole rectangle, then take away the three white triangles, each with a right angle at a corner of the rectangle." Check: 18 + 18 + 4 + 20 = 60. Common error: forgetting one of the three white triangles.

p5l4-teachsame.note: Minutes 58.5 to 60. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5, a triangle of 24 cm² with a base of 12 cm). Think-aloud: "The area is half of base times height, so base times height is DOUBLE the area: 60. Now I need two numbers that multiply to 60, and I can list them in order: 1 and 60, 2 and 30, 3 and 20, 4 and 15, 5 and 12, 6 and 10." On the worksheet they use the same idea with a different area. All the triangles lean in different ways but share the same area: link to same base and same height.

p5l4-ws2.note: Minutes 60 to 70. Children work alone on Q5 and Q4; Q3 is take-home (starred). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who give the area of a rectangle by forgetting the 1/2. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q5 and Q4, then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 70 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l4-ws2ans.note: Minutes 70 to 73. One child explains Q4; click through the rest (Q3 is take-home, its answer is here for you). Click after a child explains. Q3: ABC = 1/2 × 14 × 5 = 35 and ACD = 1/2 × 14 × 3 = 21; 35 + 21 = 56. Q4: rectangle 12 × 8 = 96; ADE = 1/2 × 4 × 8 = 16; EBF = 1/2 × 8 × 4 = 16; FCD = 1/2 × 4 × 12 = 24; 96 − 16 − 16 − 24 = 40. Q5: 1/2 × 8 × 6 = 24; 1/2 × 12 × height = 24 gives height 4 (check: 1/2 × 12 × 4 = 24); any pair with base × height = 48, such as 6 and 8, 16 and 3, 24 and 2.

p5l4-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) 9 cm A2) 96 cm² (1/2 × 12 × 16) A3) 8 cm (the square is 36 cm², and 1/2 × 9 × 8 = 36). A4) 42 cm² (84 − 42)

p5l4-stretch2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) 9 cm A2) 96 cm² (1/2 × 12 × 16) A3) 8 cm (the square is 36 cm², and 1/2 × 9 × 8 = 36). A4) 42 cm² (84 − 42)

p5l4-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 12 cm (area 1/2 × 15 × 20 = 150 cm², and 1/2 × 25 × 12 = 150) B2) 50 cm² both times: it is always half of the big square (box it in a rectangle and take away three right-angled triangles: 160 − 50 − 12 − 48 = 50, and 140 − 50 − 12 − 28 = 50) B3) 18 cm² (the height is 9 cm because 1/2 × 12 × 9 = 54; ABD has base 4 cm and the same height) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Draw a rectangle, label its sides, and join points to make a shaded triangle. Work out its area, then swap with a partner. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l4-gofurther2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 12 cm (area 1/2 × 15 × 20 = 150 cm², and 1/2 × 25 × 12 = 150) B2) 50 cm² both times: it is always half of the big square (box it in a rectangle and take away three right-angled triangles: 160 − 50 − 12 − 48 = 50, and 140 − 50 − 12 − 28 = 50) B3) 18 cm² (the height is 9 cm because 1/2 × 12 × 9 = 54; ABD has base 4 cm and the same height) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Draw a rectangle, label its sides, and join points to make a shaded triangle. Work out its area, then swap with a partner. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l4-gofurther3.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 12 cm (area 1/2 × 15 × 20 = 150 cm², and 1/2 × 25 × 12 = 150) B2) 50 cm² both times: it is always half of the big square (box it in a rectangle and take away three right-angled triangles: 160 − 50 − 12 − 48 = 50, and 140 − 50 − 12 − 28 = 50) B3) 18 cm² (the height is 9 cm because 1/2 × 12 × 9 = 54; ABD has base 4 cm and the same height) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Draw a rectangle, label its sides, and join points to make a shaded triangle. Work out its area, then swap with a partner. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l4-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are NOT on the workbook. Answers: 1) 45 cm² (rectangle 120; white triangles ABM 30, MCN 15, NDA 30; 120 − 75 = 45). 2) 50 cm² (square 100; four white corner triangles of 12.5 each make 50; PQRS is half of the square).

p5l4-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? Which triangles have a square corner? Can you find the area of the shaded part by taking away? What do you know about the four corner triangles in E2? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l4-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: M and N are middle points, so MC = 5, CN = 6, DN = 6. Each white triangle has a square corner at a corner of the rectangle. Check: 30 + 15 + 30 + 45 = 120 ✓. E2: each corner triangle has two sides of 5 cm at a right angle; a second way to see E2 is to cut the square along the diagonals of PQRS: PQRS is made of 4 triangles that are the same as the corner ones, so PQRS is exactly half.

p5l4-talk.note: Minutes 73 to 78.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: No. Two triangles with the same base and the same height have the same area, even if one leans over and has much longer sides. The area depends on the base and the height, not on the slanting sides. A long, thin triangle can have a smaller area than a short, wide one. Ask: "Can you draw a triangle with one very long side and a tiny area?" (Yes: a long base with a tiny height.) Praise reasons, not only answers. Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l4-exit.note: Minutes 78.5 to 82. Answer: 7 cm (1/2 × 12 × height = 42, so 6 × height = 42) Extension: On a grid, draw as many different triangles as you can with area 6 cm² using a base of 4 cm. Where can the top corner go? (Anywhere on the line 3 cm above the base.)

p5l4-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 82 to 84.5. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 84.5 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
